summary.text: Hawking radiation is thermal radiation released outside a black hole's event horizon through quantum effects, in a model developed by Stephen Hawking in 1974.
It carries away mass and energy, so black holes that gain nothing else are expected to shrink and vanish, very slowly for all but the smallest.
Its temperature is inversely proportional to mass, so tiny black holes would radiate more and end in a burst of high-energy radiation that has not yet been detected.

They radiate identically
The tiny one, since temperature falls as mass rises

paragraphs.heading: Light from a black hole
paragraphs.text: Hawking radiation is radiation given off outside a black hole's event horizon because of quantum effects, in a model Stephen Hawking put forward in 1974. The event horizon is the boundary past which not even light can get out, so an outside observer cannot see or be affected by anything inside it. Earlier models had assumed that radiation inside the horizon could never leave, so they did not predict this glow at all. It is expected to be extremely faint, far below what today's best telescopes can detect.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea came together
paragraphs.text: In 1971 the Soviet physicists Yakov Zeldovich and Alexei Starobinsky argued that spinning black holes should create and give off particles, reasoning from spinning metal spheres. In 1972 Jacob Bekenstein proposed that a black hole has entropy in proportion to its surface area, and so it should also have a temperature. Hawking at first disagreed, treating black holes as simple objects without entropy. After meeting Zeldovich in Moscow in 1973, he combined these ideas using quantum field theory and general relativity, and in 1974 showed that in theory a black hole radiates like a blackbody.

paragraphs.heading: Where the particles come from
paragraphs.text: The radiation has its origin in what are called vacuum fluctuations. A fluctuation in the electromagnetic field can produce a pair of photons, one outside the horizon and its partner inside, and the horizon lets them go their separate ways. The particles that escape carry energy away from the black hole. Because of Bekenstein's part in the story, the effect is also called Bekenstein–Hawking radiation.

paragraphs.heading: Temperature and size
paragraphs.text: Hawking's prediction gives the temperature as T = ℏc³/8πGMk_B, in which M stands for the black hole's mass, G for the gravitational constant, c for light speed, ℏ for the reduced Planck constant and k_B for the Boltzmann constant. That temperature, called the Hawking temperature, goes down as the mass goes up. So very small black holes should radiate more strongly than large ones and lose their mass faster for their size.

paragraphs.heading: Black holes that evaporate
paragraphs.text: Hawking radiation would drain a black hole's mass and its rotational energy, a process called black hole evaporation. A black hole that gains no mass in other ways is therefore expected to shrink and finally disappear. For all but the smallest black holes, this takes an extremely long time.

paragraphs.heading: A final flash
paragraphs.text: If small black holes exist, as the idea of primordial black holes allows, they would lose mass faster and faster as they shrink. The end would be a burst of high-energy radiation and nothing else. No such bursts have been detected yet. Since 1974, Hawking and others have checked the result mathematically by other routes, such as path integrals.
